groups.instructions: Read the report about a timetable change and answer the questions.
groups.passage:
A transport office thought a morning bus was arriving at the interchange too early. It arrived five minutes before its scheduled departure from the interchange. A dispatcher proposed holding the bus at the depot for those five minutes instead, so it would spend less time waiting at the crowded interchange. The office asked a few regular riders to keep diaries before making the change permanent.

One rider's entry showed what the office had missed. She used those five minutes to cross the square and board a second bus. The timetable displayed the arrival of one vehicle and the departure of the next as separate events. Her diary recorded the walk between them, including the wait at two pedestrian crossings. A rider who used a walking stick noted that the transfer was already tight.

The office kept the first bus's morning time but moved its five-minute pause to a later stop on the route, after most connecting passengers had got off. It also began asking passengers about the whole journey when it tested timetable changes. A bus could complete its own route efficiently while making a passenger's journey less reliable.

questions.question_text: Why did the office initially consider a later departure from the depot?

options.text: A second bus was routinely departing five minutes behind schedule.
The bus appeared to spend five minutes idle at the interchange.
The pedestrian crossings had been closed in the morning.
Passengers had asked for less time between connecting services.

questions.question_text: What did the diary reveal that the published times left out?

options.text: The number of stops each vehicle had made before arrival.
The cost of using two separate tickets.
The first bus's total time from its initial stop.
The time needed to walk from one vehicle to the next.

questions.question_text: In “the transfer was already tight,” what does “tight” mean?

options.text: Restricting how many people could board.
Following a route with narrow streets.
Difficult to describe clearly on paper.

questions.question_text: How did the office ultimately handle the five-minute pause?

options.text: It removed the morning bus from the timetable entirely.
It added the pause before the bus entered the interchange.
It moved the pause to a stop beyond the interchange.
It shifted both buses five minutes later.

questions.question_text: What principle best reflects the last paragraph?

options.text: Shorten waiting times at each stop by the same amount.
Judge a timetable mainly by how quickly the first bus reaches its final stop.
Evaluate the connections people rely on as well as the performance of individual routes.
Give drivers different routes every time passengers report a delay.

groups.instructions: Read the essay about evidence in family photographs and answer the questions.
groups.passage:
A girl assembling a family album found a photograph of her grandfather holding a large fish beside a river. Her father remembered that it was taken after a fishing contest. Her aunt insisted that the fish came from a market and that the picture had been a joke. Both remembered the smile, which the girl herself would have described as proud.

They brought the picture to a cousin who lived near the river. He recognised a fence and a willow tree, but said the family had visited that spot many times. The fence established a place, not an occasion. On the reverse, the girl found the name of a photograph shop and a date that referred to when the print was made. Even that date could be later than the day the camera was used.

The girl eventually wrote a caption with two parts. It said where the photograph was probably taken, and it recorded both explanations for the fish. The people who had given the explanations were identified by relation to the family, so a later reader could ask them about their accounts. A photo historian visiting the school liked the distinction. She said an image can preserve an appearance very clearly while leaving the reason for it outside the frame.

The girl now reads the smile differently. It still looks proud to her, but she can imagine someone smiling in the same way as part of a joke. The caption lets the image keep both possibilities until a better clue turns up.

questions.question_text: What did the father and aunt disagree about?

options.text: Whether the grandfather smiled when the picture was taken.
Which print shop made the copy.
Whether the river was visible behind the fence.
How the grandfather came to be holding the fish.

questions.question_text: Why did recognising the fence fail to resolve the disagreement?

options.text: The fence had been moved to the market after the contest.
The fence was built after the picture was printed.
The same spot had been used on many occasions.
The cousin could not remember living near any river.

questions.question_text: What did the date on the back record?

options.text: When the grandfather caught the fish.
When the family added the photograph to the album.

questions.question_text: What does “the distinction” refer to in paragraph three?

options.text: The difference between a photograph shop and a market stall.
The separation of likely location from alternative accounts of what happened.
The way relatives were ordered from oldest to youngest.
The difference between smiling for a camera and refusing to be photographed.

questions.question_text: Why did the girl identify who supplied each explanation?

options.text: It made the cousin's account more authoritative than the aunt's.
A future reader could follow up and ask the source for more information.
It helped her choose which explanation would fit on the album page.
It showed that only the family members present could read the caption.

questions.question_text: Which statement reflects the photo historian's point?

options.text: An image must include a written date to show what a person looked like.
A clear photograph gives a complete account of anything inside its frame.
The person behind the camera is the only reliable source about a photograph.
A picture may show clearly what something looked like without showing why it happened.

questions.question_text: Which title best captures the essay?

options.text: How to Find the Best Photograph Shop by the River.
A Family Argument Settled by a Smile.
Why Printed Dates Always Identify the Moment of a Photograph.
What a Family Photograph Can Tell Us, and What It Leaves Open.

groups.instructions: Read the article about changes to a school playground and answer the questions.
groups.passage:
A primary school replaced one large open court with three smaller activity areas. Staff expected a wider range of games because children no longer had to compete for the same space. After the first week, they found that most of the same ball games continued in the largest area. Some pupils who used to watch from the edge of the old court now stood between two of the new zones.

A researcher asked two pupils to show her where they usually went at break. They chose a strip under a staircase where several classmates had arranged loose wooden blocks into a row. The strip was not a marked activity area. It let the group leave the row in place while deciding what it would become: a shop counter on Monday, a bridge on Wednesday. In parts of the yard used for fast games, anything left on the ground was quickly moved for safety.

The staff changed one rule. Blocks could stay in a small sheltered area until the end of the next break, as long as there was a clear way through. They also put a box of short planks and cloth there. Some children built with the materials immediately. Others mostly watched for three breaks and then joined a game they had seen developing. The researcher counted those children separately from children who had left the area, because watching could be a step toward taking part.

This did not make balls less popular. In the larger zone, some pupils wanted to run and practise throwing. The new arrangements worked when both activities had room. Staff who had originally counted the number of zones began recording which games continued across breaks, which needed to be reset, and how children who preferred to watch could get involved.

questions.question_text: What happened in the largest of the three new zones during the first week?

options.text: It was reserved exclusively for pupils who wanted to watch.
Many of the earlier ball games continued there.
Large wooden constructions stayed there throughout every day.
Few children were willing to play there at all.

questions.question_text: Why did the strip under the staircase suit the block games?

options.text: It was the place where staff encouraged the fastest games.
The children could leave an unfinished arrangement there and return to it.
The space was officially marked for building bridges.
It came with instructions telling pupils what they could build.

questions.question_text: According to the account, how did the row of blocks serve different purposes?

options.text: The same arrangement could represent different things on different days.
A teacher rebuilt it each time the pupils changed games.
It separated the fastest runners from younger pupils.
It recorded how many games each pupil had watched.

questions.question_text: What condition limited the new rule allowing blocks to remain?

options.text: Only one child could use the blocks at a time.
The blocks had to remain in one straight line.
All pupils in the area had to join the same game.
A passage through the area had to remain open.

questions.question_text: Why did the researcher distinguish watchers from children who had left?

options.text: Watching could lead to joining a game later.
Watchers were chiefly waiting for the ball area to reopen.
Only watchers were permitted to use short planks.
Children who left always went to play a faster game.

questions.question_text: What does “reset” mean in the last paragraph?

options.text: Move to a larger area so that more pupils can join.
Record the final score for the first time.
Change the written rules without telling the players.
Set up again after the materials or arrangement had been cleared.

questions.question_text: Which observation would best reveal whether a space supports games that develop over time?

options.text: Track whether a group can resume and adapt the same game over several breaks.
Measure how quickly children cross the yard during one break.
Count how many signs identify the official zones.
Ask teachers which ball games need the largest playing surface.

questions.question_text: What is the main point of the article?

options.text: Playground designers should replace every ball court with a sheltered building area.
A playground needs the same rule about objects in every zone.
Different forms of play depend on what children can do and leave in a space, beyond how many zones are marked.
The biggest zone always provides the widest range of activities.
